clue.text: Floor covering exchanged for sack cloth?

indicators.note: covering says the word for floor lies over the other piece, going round its outside as a carpet covers boards

parts.note: a deck is the floor of a ship or a bus, and to deck someone is also to floor them

indicators.note: exchanged says the letters of the short word after it swap places with one another

parts.note: taken as written, before its letters change places

explanation.surface: Someone has swapped their carpet for a length of coarse hessian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanged' swaps the letters of 'for' to make FRO, and 'covering' sets the floor word round it. The surface runs 'sack' and 'cloth' together as rough fabric, but the cloth is the clergy and to sack is to dismiss.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an old name for the clergy, so sacking a cleric means stripping a priest of office, which this verb names.

clue.text: Trifling in amateur work, not very well

indicators.note: in says the word for trifling sits inside the letters that stand for amateur work

parts.note: DIY, short for do-it-yourself, is home repair done by amateurs instead of tradesmen
trifling means small, of little size or importance

explanation.surface: Someone has been dabbling in unpaid jobs and making a poor fist of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts SMALL inside DIY, the British abbreviation for do-it-yourself home improvement. 'Trifling' reads as a verb, dabbling, but is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something in a gloomy or feeble manner is to do it badly; both are adverbial, so one replaces the other.

clue.text: An MP's power, given little in advance

indicators.note: in says the pieces for power and little sit together inside the word for advance

parts.note: to foster a cause is to advance it, to help it develop
a reign is a period of power or rule
mini means little, as in a mini version of something

explanation.surface: A politician's authority was handed over, in small part, ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the words for power and little, which 'given' sets side by side, inside FOSTER, 'advance' as a verb meaning promote. In Britain a foreign minister is normally a Member of Parliament, which is all the definition claims.
explanation.definitionFit: In a parliamentary system the cabinet member handling overseas affairs normally sits in the legislature, so the office-holder is one example of a Member of Parliament.

clue.text: Sports car maker's lead-free vehicle

indicators.note: lead-free, read as free of its lead, says the car maker's name goes without the letter at its front

parts.note: Morgan is a British firm that builds hand-made sports cars in Malvern

explanation.surface: A sports car manufacturer has brought out a model that runs on unleaded petrol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead-free' takes the M off MORGAN, a British maker of hand-built sports cars; the lead is the front, not the metal. The vehicle is no car: it is a medium for opinion, as a party newspaper is.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper that carries a group's views is a medium or channel for them, the figurative sense both nouns share.

clue.text: In strip poker, being completely undressed leads to sex

indicators.note: undressing a word takes off its outside letters, and doing so completely strips layer after layer until only the centre is left

parts.note: it is an old euphemism for sex, as in 'doing it'; leads to only says this piece follows on from the first

explanation.surface: In a card game where losers shed their clothes, ending up naked results in lovemaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being completely undressed' peels 'poker' down to its central K, and 'leads to' only links that to IT. A strip is the British term for a sports team's matching outfit, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In British sport a team's matching shirts, shorts and socks go by either name, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: "Blind" is not a word to say

parts.note: 'Not a word!' is an order to keep quiet, and so is 'Sh!'
to say something is to utter it

explanation.surface: A speaker insists that 'blind' is a term nobody ought to use.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks belong to the surface only. 'Not a word' looks like a verdict on the term, but read as a command it is a call for silence.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are screens fitted over a window to keep out the light, so the two nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: Led, as a bird would in race

indicators.note: in says the letters for 'a bird would' sit together inside the word for race

parts.note: to race is to speed, to move very fast
a rhea is a large flightless bird of South America
would shrinks to 'd after a noun or pronoun, as in he'd, so it gives just a D

explanation.surface: Someone was out in front, the way a bird would be in a running contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts A RHEA'D inside SPEED: 'a bird would' is read as the contraction 'a rhea'd', so 'would' supplies only its D. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at the front of an attack or campaign is to head it, so the past tenses are synonyms.

clue.text: University bar near a free city

indicators.note: free means let loose, so the letters of the three words before it are released from their order

parts.note: taken as written; all three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A student union pub stands close to a self-governing town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' follows its fodder and rearranges BAR NEAR A into RBAN AREA, which goes after the U. In the surface a free city is a self-governing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A built-up district of dense streets and housing is what a town or metropolis is, so one describes the other.

clue.text: Bumpy or flatter things might conflict?

indicators.note: bumpy means uneven and jolting, so the letters of the three words after it are jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; all three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Uneven objects and smoother ones may not sit well together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bumpy' rearranges OR FLATTER THINGS. 'Might' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for power, so a 'might conflict' is a contest of power.
explanation.definitionFit: Might as a noun is power or force and a conflict is a contest, so the phrase names a contest of power.

clue.text: Queen of a country in revolution

indicators.note: in revolution says the two pieces before it are turned right round and read from the far end

parts.note: Niger is a country in West Africa

explanation.surface: A monarch reigns over a nation in the middle of an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in revolution' turns A NIGER right round; 'of' is a link. Regina is Latin for queen, the R in a British queen's cypher such as ER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for a reigning female monarch, used in her official title and in the names of British court cases.

clue.text: Starts to show girl clothing for baby

indicators.note: clothing says the two opening letters dress the other piece, one going on either side of it
Starts to asks for the letter that begins each of the two words after it

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of, as in the pros and cons

explanation.surface: Someone begins showing a girl some outfits meant for an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' picks S and G, and 'clothing', a verb here and no garment, sets them either side of PRO. Sprog is informal British for a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a small child or infant, so a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: In making 3000 from 1000, 1000 is shaky

indicators.note: In, at the head of the clue, says the last number sits inside the phrase about the sum

parts.note: turning one thousand into three thousand is trebling it, multiplying by three
M is the Roman numeral for one thousand

explanation.surface: In a sum that turns one thousand into three thousand, the starting figure looks unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts M inside TREBLING. Only the second 1000 is a Roman numeral; the first belongs to the phrase describing a multiplication by three.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that quivers or shakes is unsteady, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Unfriendly person's absurd rationale

indicators.note: absurd means making no sense, so the letters of the word after it are put in a senseless new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hostile individual gives a ridiculous justification for their behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurd' rearranges the nine letters of RATIONALE. The 's after 'person' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who estranges others and turns them hostile is hardly a friend, so the phrase describes such an individual.

clue.text: Matt Newton's new camping gear

indicators.note: new says the letters of the name before it are put into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the s after the apostrophe included

explanation.surface: A man called Matt Newton has just bought some equipment for sleeping outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' follows its fodder and rearranges MATT NEWTONS, the possessive s included. The name belongs to nobody in particular and is there for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Small shelters that sleep a pair of people are equipment for a trip under canvas, an example of such kit.

clue.text: Material written in testimony, longhand

indicators.note: written in says the letters wanted are spelt out in order within the two words that follow

explanation.surface: Relevant evidence has been set down by hand in a witness statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written in' points to five consecutive letters that run across the comma between the two words. 'Material' reads as relevant evidence but is a fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic fibre used for stockings, ropes and parachutes, so one example of a fabric.

clue.text: Cause of sand moving around in lord of the rings

indicators.note: around says the letters in the title that follows are sent round into different places

parts.note: taken as written; the title of Tolkien's novel supplies all the letters

explanation.surface: Something is shifting the sand about in Tolkien's fantasy epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges the letters of the book title, with 'in' as a link. Longshore drift is the geography term for waves striking a beach at an angle and carrying sand along the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A geography term for waves hitting a beach at an angle and carrying sediment along the coast, which is what shifts beach material.

clue.text: Round tours around welcoming hotel at Morecambe

indicators.note: welcoming says the turned word for tours opens up and takes the next two pieces in
around says the word for tours is turned round and read from its far end

parts.note: laps are tours of a circuit, as in laps of a race track
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Eric Morecambe was half of the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A circular coach trip takes in a friendly place to stay in a Lancashire seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' turns the word for tours into SPAL, and 'welcoming' opens it for the hotel letter and a first name. Morecambe is a seaside resort in Lancashire, but here it is the British comedian Eric Morecambe, who took his stage name from the town.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaped like a ball or globe, which is being circular in three dimensions, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: A child, almost completely offensive?

parts.note: a means per, for each, as in ten pounds a head
a son is someone's child

indicators.note: almost says the word for completely stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: all can mean completely, as in all alone or all covered in mud

explanation.surface: A youngster is behaving in a way that is very nearly entirely obnoxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ALL down to AL. 'A' is no article here but 'per', as in twice a day, and the question mark admits that remarks about someone's private life are only one kind of rudeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Remarks aimed at someone's private life or character are insulting, so the adjective can mean rude or hurtful.

clue.text: A clan held tight wild animals they own?

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of the four words before it are let loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; all four words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A Scottish family kept a firm grip on the untamed beasts that belonged to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' follows its fodder and rearranges A CLAN HELD TIGHT. 'They' in the definition is the clan: Highland cattle are the shaggy, long-horned breed of the Scottish Highlands, home of the clans.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaggy long-horned breed from the mountains of Scotland, where the clans live, so livestock such a family would keep.

clue.text: Failed flier is keeping wheels up half-way

indicators.note: keeping says the short word before it holds the next two pieces within itself

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car, as in a nice set of wheels

indicators.note: half-way says the short word before it gets only half-way, so just one half of it is used

explanation.surface: A pilot who flunked the test has the landing gear stuck partly retracted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts CAR, with the letter 'half-way' takes from 'up', inside the short verb before it. In Greek myth Icarus flew too near the sun on wings of wax and fell into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth he flew too close to the sun on wings of wax and feathers, which melted, and he fell into the sea.

clue.text: I call on one Catholic to return

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the three pieces before it are joined and read from right to left

parts.note: re means on in the sense of about or concerning, as in a memo re the budget
I is the Roman numeral for one
RC is the abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: The speaker urges a lapsed churchgoer to come home to the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns the whole run RE + I + RC to give CRIER. The definition is in the first person: a town crier is someone who calls out public announcements.
explanation.definitionFit: A town official who shouts out public announcements could describe the job in these two words, a first-person description.

clue.text: Those opening the van dyke show will eat 16 set meals?

indicators.note: will eat says the four opening letters swallow the other piece, taking it in among them
Those opening asks for the letter that opens each of the four words after it

parts.note: 16 points to the answer at 16 down, a word for private or intimate, and inner means the same

explanation.surface: Whoever launches the Van Dyke show is going to get through sixteen fixed-price menus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those opening' picks T, V, D and S, and 'will eat' puts INNER among them. 16 is a cross-reference, not a count of meals, and the set is a television: a TV dinner is a ready meal eaten in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-made trays of food designed for eating in front of the television, which is informally called the set.

clue.text: I refuse runs yet will run around

indicators.note: will run around says the two pieces before it go round to face the other way, read from the far end

parts.note: R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs
yet means even in comparisons: yet more is even more

explanation.surface: A batsman declines to score but is happy to jog about the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will run around' turns R + EVEN to face the other way. The definition is a reply to a demand: an emphatic 'Never!' amounts to 'I refuse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Given as a one-word reply to a demand, it is an emphatic way of declining, an exclamation with the same force.

clue.text: Regularly issued arrest warrant, lacking initial restraint

indicators.note: Regularly issued says letters of the next word are given out at even intervals, every second one
lacking initial says the word for warrant goes without the letter it begins with

parts.note: a licence is a warrant: each is a document giving official permission

explanation.surface: A court order to detain someone was routinely handed out with no early moderation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly issued' takes the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'arrest', and 'lacking initial' drops the L from LICENCE. The surface's 'arrest warrant' is split between the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding back from speaking freely is a form of self-control or reserve, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Tiller must not feature hard wood

indicators.note: must not feature says the word for tiller has to go without the letter the next word supplies

parts.note: a tiller is the lever that steers a boat, and the helm is the same steering gear
H is hard on pencils, as in HB

explanation.surface: The steering handle of a boat should not be made of dense timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must not feature' takes H out of HELM. The surface joins 'hard' to 'wood', but they do separate jobs: one is a letter, the other the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The timber of a tall deciduous tree, once widely used for coffins and boat keels, is one kind of this material.

clue.text: A particular diet for one in front

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective for this way of eating, or a noun for someone who follows it; naming the regime itself with it is the setter's shorthand

indicators.note: in says the short piece for 'for one' sits inside the word for front

parts.note: the van is the front of an advancing army or movement, short for vanguard
for one means for example, which is abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: A special eating plan has been drawn up for the person at the head of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the abbreviation inside VAN, the front of an army. 'For one' reads as 'for a single person' but means 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A regime that avoids all animal products, dairy and eggs included, is one specific way of eating.

clue.text: Shock? Not half, having left us extra

indicators.note: Not half says the word for shock is not all used: only one half of its letters stays

parts.note: a shock is a surprise, something unexpected
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asked whether they were stunned at being bequeathed more than expected, the family reply with an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it is literal: only the front half of SURPRISE is kept. 'having' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An amount beyond what is needed is spare or additional, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Curiosity here — fictional computer guide

parts.note: Curiosity is the NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2012, so Mars is where it is
HAL is the ship's computer in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey

explanation.surface: Here is something intriguing: a handbook to the computers of science fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C is honest: Curiosity is NASA's rover, not inquisitiveness. 'Guide' reads as a handbook but is a verb, to usher people into their places.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher or lead people into their proper places is to direct them, so the two verbs are synonyms.
